name: elm
desc: Functional programming language for building browser-based GUIs
why: A purely functional language with no runtime exceptions and a distinctive architecture, still unusual enough to be worth a look.

brief.what_it_is: Elm is a functional programming language that compiles to JavaScript, aimed at building websites and web apps. You write Elm source files and the compiler outputs JavaScript that runs in the browser. The official guide's sample is a counter: a Main module imports Browser, Html and Html.Events, calls Browser.sandbox with init, update and view functions, and defines a Msg type with Increment and Decrement. The guide also lists the language's promised guarantees: no runtime errors in practice, friendly error messages, reliable refactoring, and automatically enforced semantic versioning for Elm packages.
brief.why_it_exists: The guide frames Elm as a language designed for simplicity and quality tooling, and says its guarantees come from the language design itself rather than from combining JavaScript libraries. It also presents the language as a way to make web apps with more confidence, and says the ideas carry over to writing JavaScript.
brief.how_it_works: Elm uses The Elm Architecture: a program is built from an init value, an update function that takes a Msg and the current model and returns a new model, and a view function that renders the model to HTML. The compiler turns that Elm code into JavaScript. The guide's sample shows the pattern with Browser.sandbox, which the guide presents as the entry point for a simple interactive app.
brief.install_notes: Not checked. The homepage and docs page returned only navigation text, and the guide's introduction did not cover installation in the text I read. The brew description and the executable name 'elm' are the only install facts I have.
brief.standout: Elm claims no runtime exceptions in practice, which the guide attributes to the language design rather than to a library. Its enforced semantic versioning for packages is also unusual: the compiler checks that version bumps match API changes.
brief.status: unknown. I found no release date, last-commit date, or changelog on the pages I fetched, so I cannot judge whether the project is actively maintained from this evidence.
brief.caveats: The homepage and docs pages returned almost no text, so this brief leans on the guide for the description and claims. Those claims are the project's own and I did not verify them. The guide's sample uses Browser.sandbox, and it is not clear from what I read how the current recommended entry points differ. The brew caveats field is empty.
quotes: Elm is a functional language that compiles to JavaScript. It helps you make websites and web apps.
If you are on the fence, I can safely guarantee that if you give Elm a shot and actually make a project in it, you will end up writing better JavaScript code.

judge.reason: Elm’s functional design, compiler-enforced package versioning, and distinctive architecture make building browser apps a genuinely instructive language experiment.

entry.title: Elm
entry.tldr: A small functional language that compiles to JavaScript, built around one architecture and a promise of no runtime errors in practice.
entry.deeper_look:
Elm is a functional language for websites and web apps. You write Elm source files and the compiler outputs JavaScript that runs in the browser. The official guide describes it as "a functional language that compiles to JavaScript. It helps you make websites and web apps."

Every Elm program follows The Elm Architecture. There is a model, an `init` value, an `update` function that takes a message and the current model and returns a new model, and a `view` function that renders the model to HTML. The guide's sample is a counter: a `Msg` type with `Increment` and `Decrement`, wired together with `Browser.sandbox`.

The guide says Elm's guarantees come from the language design, not from stacking JavaScript libraries. It lists them: no runtime errors in practice, friendly error messages, reliable refactoring, and enforced semantic versioning for packages. That last one means the compiler checks that a version bump matches the API change.

The larger idea is that state, change and display can be separated this cleanly, and that a compiler can enforce it. The guide claims these ideas carry over to JavaScript, and that a real Elm project will leave you "writing better JavaScript code." That is the project's own claim, not something checked here.

try_this.what_happens: Lists the compiler's subcommands, a first look at what the tool can do.

entry.whats_unique: The language promises no runtime errors in practice, and its package manager has the compiler enforce semantic versioning against actual API changes.
entry.caveats: The brief found no release dates or commit history, so whether Elm is actively maintained is unknown, and the guarantees quoted are the project's own claims.
